_comment: DEMO DATA. Every record here is fictional. EMPLIDs are in a reserved 99xxxxxx
block and every email uses the .invalid TLD (RFC 2606) so no record here can be
This file is the whole development dataset. It conforms to the canonical schema
in src/lib/canonical.ts — run `npm run test` after editing and the validation
test will tell you if a record drifted.
Scenario coverage is documented in docs/canonical-schema.md and asserted in
src/lib/fixtures.test.ts. If you remove a student, check that test first: each
one is carrying a display state the UI needs to handle.
`careerActions` is the action catalog: every recommended action defined once,
with a stable id. `careerMaps` places them in terms for everyone; `careerTracks`
layer specialisations on top by adding, moving or excluding placements. Student
progress is keyed on the action id and never on the track, which is what lets a
student change track without losing credit for what they have already done.

careerActions.title: Meet your department advisor and walk through the four-year plan
careerActions.why: The plan only works if you know what is on it, and this is the meeting that puts a face to the person who signs off on everything later.

careerActions.title: Complete the FOCUS 2 career self-assessment
careerActions.why: Most first-years pick a direction from the three job titles they have heard of. This is a cheap way to find the ones they have not.

careerActions.title: Set up your Handshake profile and upload a first resume
careerActions.why: Every campus job, workshop and employer visit is posted there. A blank profile means you never see them.

careerActions.title: Join a CS or Math student club
careerActions.why: The cheapest way to meet the people who will tell you about an internship two years from now.

careerActions.title: Go to one instructor's office hours before midterms
careerActions.why: The first visit is the hard one. Recommendation letters come from faculty who can picture your face.

careerActions.title: Attend two Math/CS seminar talks
careerActions.why: Seeing what research and industry work actually look like is how a vague major turns into a direction.

careerActions.title: Create a LinkedIn profile
careerActions.why: Alumni and recruiters look you up before they reply. No result is worse than a thin one.

careerActions.title: Create a GitHub account and push your coursework to it
careerActions.why: Four years of commits is a record of how you work that no resume line can fake.

careerActions.title: Use the Collaborative Learning Center at least once
careerActions.why: Students who get help early keep the GPA that keeps every later door open.

careerActions.title: Submit one Scholarship Center application
careerActions.why: An hour of writing against a few hundred dollars is the best hourly rate on campus.

careerActions.title: Build and deploy one small project
careerActions.why: The first thing you can send someone a link to is worth more than the next three courses on your transcript.

careerActions.title: Work through one free online course in something you are curious about
careerActions.why: Summer is the only term with room to follow curiosity instead of a syllabus.

careerActions.title: Line up campus or local paid work for the fall
careerActions.why: Paid work you can get to on the train beats an unpaid internship you cannot afford to take.

careerActions.title: Go to a resume workshop with Career Services
careerActions.why: Resume conventions in tech change every couple of years, and the people who read them run this workshop.

careerActions.title: Get your resume reviewed until it is complete
careerActions.why: A resume nobody but you has read is a first draft.

careerActions.title: Go to the fall career fair, even with nothing to apply for yet
careerActions.why: Going once with nothing at stake is what makes the junior-year one survivable.

careerActions.title: Apply to sophomore pipeline programs — Google STEP and Microsoft Explore open in August and September
careerActions.why: These are the main funnel into junior-year internships now, and hardly any sophomore applies because nobody tells them to.

careerActions.title: Semester check-in with your advisor
careerActions.why: Twenty minutes a term is what keeps a small problem from becoming a lost semester.

careerActions.title: Apply to CUNY Tech Prep — applications close in March
careerActions.why: Free, CUNY-only, a year long, with an employer network attached. There is no better-value application on this list.

careerActions.title: Interview a York alum in your field for thirty minutes
careerActions.why: Alumni answer students. The same email from a stranger goes unread.

careerActions.title: Apply to at least five summer internships or research programs
careerActions.why: The first round of applications is practice. Spend it in sophomore year rather than junior year.

careerActions.title: Look into paid NYC programs — Break Through Tech AI and NYC LSAMP
careerActions.why: Both are paid, both are local, and neither asks you to fund a summer in another city.

careerActions.title: Interview prep sprint: data-structures problems and one mock interview
careerActions.why: Junior-year postings open in August. Preparation that starts in September has started late.

careerActions.title: Start a portfolio page — one good README counts
careerActions.why: Somewhere to point at is the difference between saying you can build things and showing it.

careerActions.title: Build a list of twenty employers and the month each one opens applications
careerActions.why: Recruiting is a calendar, not a search. Miss the window and the best-fit job was never really an option.

careerActions.title: Apply to summer internships — most postings open August through October and close rolling
careerActions.why: Rolling means the last week of the window is nothing like the first. Early applications get read by people.

careerActions.title: Work the fall career fair with a thirty-second pitch ready
careerActions.why: The pitch is the whole event. Everything else is standing in line.

careerActions.title: Confirm your graduation plan with your advisor
careerActions.why: A missing requirement found in junior year is an inconvenience. Found in senior spring it is a semester.

careerActions.title: Join a professional association — ACM, NSBE, SHPE or a women-in-computing chapter
careerActions.why: Student membership costs a few dollars and the job boards behind it are not public.

careerActions.title: Do a mock interview with Career Services
careerActions.why: The first technical interview should not be one that counts.

careerActions.title: Identify two people who would write you a strong recommendation
careerActions.why: Knowing who they are is what lets you give them two months' notice instead of two weeks'.

careerActions.title: Do two more informational interviews in your target field
careerActions.why: Two conversations tell you more about a role than twenty job postings.

careerActions.title: Complete an internship, research placement or a substantial project
careerActions.why: This is the line every reader of your resume looks for first.

careerActions.title: Rewrite your resume around what you did this summer
careerActions.why: The work is only worth what you can describe. Write it down while you still remember the details.

careerActions.title: Apply to new-grad roles — postings open August through October, the same as internships
careerActions.why: New-grad hiring runs a year ahead of the start date. Waiting for spring means applying to what is left.

careerActions.title: Submit graduate school applications — most CS deadlines fall December 1-15
careerActions.why: Everything a graduate application needs takes longer than you think, and all of it is due at once.

careerActions.title: Ask your recommenders formally, at least a month before the deadline
careerActions.why: A good letter takes time. A rushed one reads like a rushed one.

careerActions.title: Final advising meeting: graduation check and the plan after it
careerActions.why: The last meeting is where someone checks that the plan survives contact with reality.

careerActions.title: Bring any offer to an advisor before you accept it
careerActions.why: Compensation, start date and what you will actually be doing are all negotiable, and nobody tells students that.

careerActions.title: Update LinkedIn and your portfolio with your final project work
careerActions.why: The version of you an employer finds should be the version that just graduated.

careerActions.title: Connect with the York alumni network before you graduate
careerActions.why: Access is easiest while you are still a student, and you will want it in three years.

careerActions.title: Do a hackathon — free ones run across NYC most months
careerActions.why: A weekend is enough to ship something, and the people you build it with become your network.

careerActions.title: Work through 150+ data-structures and algorithms problems
careerActions.why: Technical screens test a narrow skill that only repetition builds. Start the summer before, not the week before.

careerActions.title: Make two contributions to an open-source project you actually use
careerActions.why: Public code review by strangers is the closest thing to on-the-job experience you can get for free.

careerActions.title: Work through a system design primer and build one project that handles real load
careerActions.why: Every new-grad backend loop asks how you would scale it, and the answer is learnable.

careerActions.title: Take linear algebra and probability as early as your schedule allows
careerActions.why: Every machine learning course you will want later assumes both, and taking them late costs a year.

careerActions.title: Email three professors about openings in their labs
careerActions.why: Getting into a lab by sophomore year is the one action that makes everything else on this track possible.

careerActions.title: Apply to NSF REU sites — deadlines cluster in February
careerActions.why: Paid summer research with housing included, and the application is mostly one essay you reuse.

careerActions.title: Present a poster or write up a workshop paper
careerActions.why: Applications ask what you have done, and 'worked in a lab' is not an answer until something came out of it.

careerActions.title: Consider the NSF GRFP — the CISE deadline is in late October
careerActions.why: Three years of funding, seniors are eligible, and most of them never hear about it.

careerActions.title: Work through probability and mental-arithmetic problem sets
careerActions.why: Quant interviews test probability under time pressure, and there is no shortcut but practice.

careerActions.title: Take the heaviest mathematics sequence you can carry
careerActions.why: Quant hiring screens on mathematical maturity before it screens on anything else.

careerActions.title: Apply to sophomore quant programs — Jane Street, SIG and Citadel run them in February and March
careerActions.why: These are the entry point to junior-year quant internships, and the deadlines land in sophomore spring.

careerActions.title: Enter a trading competition or a Kaggle contest
careerActions.why: A ranked finish is evidence that survives a resume screen.

students.bio: Returning student, second career. Twelve years in clinical laboratory work before enrolling. Brings domain knowledge most of the cohort does not have, and is still catching up on the engineering fundamentals that the traditional-age students picked up in their first two years.

goal.statement: I want to build the tools that clinical labs actually use. Most of the software I worked with for twelve years was designed by people who had never set foot in a lab, and it showed — workflows that took four clicks should have taken one, alerts that everybody learned to ignore, exports that silently dropped the last row. I know exactly what is wrong with those products and I want to be the person in the room who can say so and then go implement the fix.
goal.timeline: Graduating December 2026, looking to start immediately
goal.advisorNotes: The clearest articulation of a goal I have heard this year. Her problem is not direction, it is that she undersells the lab experience on paper.

skills.evidence: Twelve years of LIMS query work

skills.evidence: Twelve years as a medical laboratory technologist

skills.evidence: Wrote SOPs and validation reports professionally

skills.evidence: Used for assay statistics at previous employer

requiredSkills.rationale: Non-negotiable in this sector, and she already has it.

requiredSkills.name: Model deployment
requiredSkills.rationale: The Docker work is the start of this.

requiredSkills.name: Regulatory submission process
requiredSkills.rationale: FDA pathway literacy for diagnostic products.

artifacts.advisorNotes: Third draft. Still buries the lab experience on page two — that experience is the whole differentiator and it needs to be at the top.
Capstone is there, needs a README.

notes.content:
Long session, about ninety minutes, and worth recording properly because it changed how I am going to advise her.

She came in convinced that her twelve years in the clinical lab are a liability — that employers will read the gap between her associate's degree in 2011 and her enrollment here in 2023 as a sign she is behind, and that she needs to compensate by looking as much like a traditional new graduate as possible. Her résumé reflects that belief: the lab work is compressed into four lines on the second page under "Additional Experience", and the first page is her coursework and two class projects.

I pushed back hard on this. For a general software engineering role she might be right that the gap needs explaining. For the specific role she is targeting — applied ML on clinical systems — the lab experience is not a gap to explain, it is the entire reason a hiring manager would pick her over a twenty-two year old with a better GPA. She has validated assays. She knows what a false positive costs when a real patient is on the other end of it. She has been the person who had to work around badly designed software at two in the morning. There are maybe four people in this year's cohort who could speak credibly to any of that and she is the only one who can speak to all of it.

Action items agreed: she rewrites the résumé with the lab experience first and the degree as supporting context, not the other way round. She drafts three sentences describing a specific software failure she worked around, to use as an interview story. I am connecting her with an alum at a diagnostics company — sent the introduction email after the session.

She was not fully convinced by the end. Noting that here so I remember to check whether the rewrite actually happened or whether she reverted to the old framing.
Capstone topic approved — anomaly detection on lab instrument output. Good alignment with her target role.
Referred to the writing centre for graduate school application essays. She later decided against applying.

milestones.description: Faculty-supervised. Presented to the department in August. The autoencoder approach caught two instrument drift events that the existing rule-based system missed.
